stem: A parent asks whether an out-of-range newborn screening result means the baby definitely has the condition. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: No. Newborn screening identifies babies who may have a condition; an out-of-range result usually requires timely follow-up and often diagnostic testing
options.B: Yes. Newborn screening is diagnostic, so an out-of-range result confirms the condition without additional testing
options.C: No. Out-of-range newborn screening results can be ignored unless the baby develops symptoms
options.D: Yes. Newborn screening is performed only when a baby already has symptoms or a strong family history

rationale: HRSA explains that newborn screening and diagnostic testing are not the same. Screening checks whether a newborn might have certain serious conditions and is intended to connect affected infants with early care. An out-of-range screen does not by itself establish the diagnosis; timely follow-up, often including diagnostic testing, is needed. Waiting for symptoms can delay treatment for conditions in which early intervention matters. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Explain that newborn screening identifies risk rather than confirming diagnosis and that out-of-range results require timely follow-up testing even when the infant appears well.

correction_summary: Replaced the generic purpose-of-screening recall question with a clinically important distinction between screening and diagnosis. Added the required follow-up action for an out-of-range result and avoided implying that all U.S. states screen for an identical condition panel.
audit_findings: A directly reflects HRSA. B falsely treats a screening result as diagnostic; C dangerously delays follow-up; D falsely restricts screening to symptomatic/high-risk infants. The item avoids state-panel variability and one clear best answer remains. Independent adversarial second pass passed.
